```{r, include = FALSE}
# eval = TRUE, unlike the other articles: every chunk here is an
# include_graphics() call whose whole purpose is to place the image.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE,
                      out.width = "100%")
```

Every figure a default run writes, shown as the unmodified output of the
demonstration cohort in [README section
2](https://github.com/bhagesh-h/cyRAVEN#2-quick-start), with what it measures and
what this particular run shows.

The cohort is two CytoTrol control acquisitions partitioned at random into eight
pseudo-samples. Three properties of it govern how every figure below reads:

**The group labels are randomised.** Every pseudo-sample comes from the same
tube, so the true between-group difference is zero. Anything reported as
significant is a false positive, and counting them measures calibration rather
than sensitivity.

**The panel carries no CD45 and no viability dye.** The parent gate is therefore
scatter and singlets rather than live leukocytes, while the axis labels and the
`pct_of_cd45_pos` column retain the CD45 naming.

**The pseudo-samples are thinned in place.** Each retains its events' original
acquisition times, so the rate profile of the source file survives into all four
of its children.

Which file each figure comes from, and which flag produces it, is in the
[Output article](outputs.html). The order to read them in is in the
[Diagnostics article](diagnostics.html) and is reproduced by `report.html`.

# 1. Before any number

## recon_diagnostics.png

The scatter gate and singlet band per sample, drawn on the distributions they
were derived from.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_recon_diagnostics.png")
```

**What to look for.** The scatter boundary should sit in the trough between the
debris mode and the intact-cell mode, and the singlet band should follow the
diagonal of FSC-H against FSC-A rather than cutting across it.

**This run.** All eight panels place the boundary in the same position on
distributions of the same shape, which is expected: they are four thinned copies
each of two files. A cohort of genuinely different donors would not look this
uniform, and uniformity here is a property of the example rather than a result.

## gating_qc.png

Every marker threshold superimposed on the density it was derived from, per
sample.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_gating_qc.png")
```

**What to look for.** A cut in the trough between two modes is well placed. A cut
on the flank of a single mode is a quantile fallback, and the frequency behind it
carries no evidence of separation. This is the only place a shoulder-placed
threshold is visible; it appears in no table.

**This run.** CD3, CD4, CD8 and CD45RA resolve a minimum in every sample. CCR7
and CD38 do not resolve one in any, and their cuts sit on the flank of a single
mode. Section 5 gives the reason.

# 2. Placement precision and counting sufficiency

## frequency_uncertainty.png

Each population's per-sample frequency with the standard uncertainty propagated
from the thresholds behind it.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_frequency_uncertainty.png")
```

**What to look for.** Whether the bar within a sample is narrower than the
scatter between samples. Where it is not, the variation on display is the cut
moving rather than the biology.

**This run.** Seven of ten populations have an uncertainty as wide as the
between-sample spread. That is the correct result here and not a warning: the
pseudo-samples come from one tube, so the between-sample spread is close to zero
by construction and gate placement is necessarily the larger term. On a real
cohort the same reading identifies populations not worth testing.

## uncertainty_budget.png

Which threshold each population's uncertainty comes from, as a median
contribution per term.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_uncertainty_budget.png")
```

**What to look for.** Which gate to fix. A population dominated by one marker has
one threshold worth inspecting; a cohort dominated by the parent term has a
parent-gate problem that no attention to the downstream markers will improve.

**This run.** The parent term enters every population because it sets the
denominator they are all expressed against, which is the concentration the
operator-variability literature reports for manually gated data as well.

## detection_limits.png

How many samples each population clears the limits of detection and
quantification in.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_detection_limits.png")
```

**What to look for.** A population mostly below the limit of quantification
cannot be recovered by re-gating: its numerator is small for want of acquired
cells, so the remedies are a longer acquisition or a higher
`--max-events-per-file`. A population split across the limit is the dangerous
case, because a group difference in it can be produced entirely by which samples
happened to clear it.

**This run.** All ten populations clear both limits in all eight samples, at
roughly 30,000 events each. This is what a well-powered run looks like; the
figure earns its place when it does not.

# 3. Are the populations what they were declared to be

## population_marker_heatmap.png

Measured marker intensity against the declared populations, z-scored across the
run.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_population_marker_heatmap.png")
```

**What to look for.** In clustering-first analysis this figure assigns identity.
Here identity is declared before the data are examined, so the figure serves the
inverse function: a column labelled CD4 T cells that does not show elevated CD4
and depressed CD8 falsifies the gate that produced it.

**This run.** The CD4 and CD8 T cell columns separate on CD4 and CD8 in the
directions the specification declares, and the memory subsets separate on CCR7
and CD45RA. The specification is not contradicted by the data it was applied to.

## population_frequencies.png

The pooled composition across samples.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_population_frequencies.png")
```

**What to look for.** Whether the composition is biologically plausible for the
material. An implausible composition is usually a specification error rather than
a finding.

**This run.** CD4 T cells at roughly 46% and CD8 T cells at roughly 21% of the
parent are ordinary values for peripheral blood T cells, which is what these
control samples are.

## cohort_composition_heatmap.png

Each group's share of every population, after normalising the groups to a common
notional cell count.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_cohort_composition_heatmap.png")
```

**What to look for.** An even split is 50%. Normalising first is what stops
unequal sample numbers or acquisition depth from generating the pattern.

**This run.** Every population sits within a few points of 50%, which is the
expected result when the group labels are randomised. The largest departure,
Activated T cells at 59/41, is the one comparison that reaches nominal
significance in section 6 and does not survive correction.

# 4. The shared embedding

## umap_overview.png

One UMAP per marker panel, computed across all samples, coloured by population
and by sample.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_umap_overview.png")
```

**What to look for.** Whether the declared populations occupy coherent regions,
and whether the sample panel shows samples overlapping rather than separating. A
sample that occupies its own territory is a batch effect or a failed
acquisition, not a biological finding.

**This run.** The samples overlap completely, as they must: they are thinned
copies of two files. The population colouring separates the T cell subsets from
the non-T cells.

## umap_overview_by_group.png

The same embedding split by study group.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_umap_overview_by_group.png")
```

**This run.** The two groups occupy the same regions in the same proportions,
which is the correct appearance for randomised labels and the visual counterpart
of the calibration result in section 6.

## umap_markers.png

The embedding coloured by each marker's intensity in turn.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_umap_markers.png")
```

**What to look for.** Whether the regions the populations occupy are the regions
that are bright for the markers defining them. This is the same audit as the
phenotype heatmap, per cell rather than per population.

**This run.** CD4 and CD8 are bright in mutually exclusive regions, and CD3 is
bright across both and dark over the non-T region.

## umap_density.png and umap_density_by_group.png

Where cells are concentrated, overall and by group.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_umap_density.png")
```

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_umap_density_by_group.png")
```

**What to look for.** Density differences between groups that the population
frequencies do not capture, which can indicate structure the specification does
not describe. `--cluster` is the test for that; this figure is the reason to run
it.

**This run.** The two group densities are indistinguishable.

## umap_multigraph_overlay.png

Subclusters within each declared population, drawn on the shared embedding.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_umap_multigraph_overlay.png")
```

**What to look for.** A declared population that splits into subclusters
responding differently is one whose aggregate frequency can report no change
while its parts move in opposite directions.

# 5. Why a threshold did not resolve

## acquisition_qc.png

Events recorded in each equal-width slice of the acquisition, one panel per
sample, with the flagged slices marked.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_acquisition_qc.png")
```

**What to look for.** A flat line is a steady acquisition. A sustained trough is
a partial clog, a spike is usually a bubble, and a step is a settings change
part-way through the tube.

**This run.** Six of eight samples carry at least one flagged slice, from 2.2% to
9.0% of their events. This is inherited rather than introduced: the
pseudo-samples are thinned in place, so the rate profile of each source
acquisition survives into all four of its children, and `donor02_rep3` and
`donor02_rep4` being the only stable pair reflects where the thinning happened to
fall.

The number that decides what to do about it is in `acquisition_qc_impact.csv`,
not in this figure. Excluding every flagged slice would move the largest
population by **0.195 percentage points**, against gate uncertainties of one to
two points for the same populations. The instability is real, and it is smaller
than the uncertainty already reported on the numbers it would affect, so no file
here needs re-acquiring. Nothing is removed unless `--drop-unstable-events` is
given.

## Spillover spreading

`spreading_receivers.csv` and `spreading_pairs.csv` have no figure; they are
ranked tables. They belong here because they answer the question section 1 left
open.

Thirteen of forty ordered channel pairs widen the receiver's negative population
by 25% or more. Two markers are flagged as a panel design problem rather than a
gating one:

| Receiver | Worst source | Widening | Fallback rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| CD38 | CD45RA | 2.21x | 1.00 |
| CCR7 | CD3 | 3.03x | 1.00 |

These are the two markers that resolved no density minimum in any sample in
`gating_qc.png`. Their negative populations are two and three times wider when
the source channel is bright, which fills in the valley a threshold would have
been placed in. No gating strategy recovers a cut that spreading has erased; the
remedy is the panel.

# 6. The results

## group_comparison.png

Per-population abundance between groups, as per-sample distributions.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_group_comparison.png")
```

**What to look for.** The reading order is adjusted p, then Cliff's delta, then
`difference_over_gate_u`, then `difference_over_total_u`. A result surviving all
four is one the run supports; the brackets on the figure show only the first.

**This run.** Of ten populations, one reaches raw *p* < 0.05 and none survives
Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Since the group labels are randomised, that is a
measurement of the false-positive rate and it is the value a correctly calibrated
test returns at ten comparisons.

The one nominal hit is instructive twice over. `compositional_concordance.csv`
classifies it as significant on raw percentages only, which is the configuration
the compositional constraint produces rather than an independent change. And in
`group_comparison_stats.csv` the Non-T cells comparison has
`difference_over_gate_u` of 2.91 against `difference_over_total_u` of 0.95:
judged on gate placement alone the difference looks resolvable, and once the
events behind it are counted it is not.

## marker_state.png

Differential state per population and marker, on per-sample values.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_marker_state.png")
```

**This run.** 140 tests, none reaching raw *p* < 0.05. Marker expression within
populations is unchanged between the randomised groups, as it must be.

## functional_markers.png

The same comparison restricted to the functional marker blocks declared in the
config.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_functional_markers.png")
```

# 7. Is the contrast confounded

## threshold_drift.png

Whether each marker's per-sample thresholds separate by study group.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/demo_threshold_drift.png")
```

**What to look for.** A flagged marker means the populations defined by it are
not identically specified across the comparison, so part of any abundance
difference is definitional rather than biological. No clustering method has an
equivalent output, because none carries a prior definition capable of drifting.

**This run.** Seven markers tested, none flagged. The thresholds do not know
which group a sample was assigned to, which is the expected result when the
assignment is random.

# What this example cannot show

The cohort has no real effect in it, so nothing here demonstrates that cyRAVEN
detects one. Every figure above is a calibration or a mechanism check. Read it
for output shape, for the reading order, and for what a correctly behaving run
looks like when the answer is nothing.
